In onboard environments characterised by high operational risk, near-miss reporting is an important mechanism for identifying latent risks, preventing accidents and supporting organisational improvement. However, there remains limited empirical understanding of whether the just culture advocated in formal systems can be translated into the lived reporting experience of seafarers who are willing, able and motivated to report near-miss incidents on a sustained basis. To address this issue, this study draws on semi-structured interviews with seafarers and shore-based managers. Six interrelated themes are identified: ease of reporting, motivation to report, trust, reporting independence, feedback and acknowledgement. The findings indicate that near-miss reporting is more likely to occur in organisational contexts where reporting is accessible, safe and worthwhile. Complicated procedures, paperwork burdens and hierarchical pressure weaken seafarers’ willingness to report, whereas simplified procedures, fair management, low exposure communication channels, timely feedback and positive acknowledgement help strengthen reporting willingness and promote experience sharing. This study provides context-specific empirical evidence on how formal just culture is translated into frontline reporting practice and offers practical insights that may inform efforts to improve near-miss reporting, reduce reporting concerns and strengthen closed-loop feedback in comparable organisational or cultural settings.

The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education has created new opportunities for supporting academic writing. AI-powered tools can provide immediate feedback on grammar, vocabulary, sentence structure, and text organisation. However, the availability of automated feedback does not guarantee that learners can evaluate its accuracy or use it effectively. This paper examines the importance of developing EFL learners’ ability to critically evaluate AI-generated feedback through a conceptual analysis of relevant literature. Previous research has investigated learners’ engagement with automated writing evaluation, their responses to ChatGPT-generated suggestions, and the effectiveness of AI feedback in comparison with teacher feedback (Yang et al., 2024; Cengiz et al., 2025; Alnemrat et al., 2025). Building on these studies and the concept of student feedback literacy (Carless & Boud, 2018), the paper proposes a four-stage pedagogical framework: analysing feedback, verifying suggestions, justifying revision decisions, and reflecting on revised texts. The framework emphasises the importance of learner judgement, teacher guidance, and responsible AI use. It may provide a basis for designing EFL academic writing activities in higher education, including the Uzbek educational context. Further empirical research is needed to evaluate its effectiveness in classroom practice. Keywords: artificial intelligence, AI-generated feedback, EFL academic writing, critical evaluation, feedback literacy, writing instruction

Résumé La littérature sur l’e-gouvernement s’est longtemps structurée autour de deux questions : le degré de sophistication des services numériques et les facteurs d’adoption par les usagers. Ces approches ont produit des modèles utiles, mais elles rendent imparfaitement compte du passage d’une offre de services en ligne à une transformation durable des organisations publiques. Cet article propose une revue intégrative visant à réexaminer cette transition à partir d’un corpus de 34 articles scientifiques publiés entre 2001 et 2026 dans des revues indexées dans Scopus et/ou Web of Science. L’analyse articule quatre courants : les modèles de maturité, les travaux sur l’adoption et la confiance, la transformation organisationnelle et l’interopérabilité, ainsi que la littérature sur la valeur publique. Trois résultats principaux émergent. Premièrement, la maturité numérique ne peut être assimilée à une trajectoire linéaire : les administrations combinent des niveaux hétérogènes de sophistication des services, d’intégration des données et de transformation interne. Deuxièmement, l’existence d’infrastructures ou de services numériques constitue une condition nécessaire mais non suffisante ; leur appropriation dépend de l’accessibilité, des compétences numériques, de la confiance, de l’utilisabilité et de l’adéquation des canaux. Troisièmement, le passage au gouvernement digital repose surtout sur des capacités organisationnelles d’intégration : leadership, gouvernance du changement, compétences, interopérabilité, coordination interorganisationnelle et apprentissage. Sur cette base, l’article propose un modèle théorique d’intégration stratégique du gouvernement digital reliant fondations sociotechniques, capacités d’appropriation, capacités organisationnelles et création de valeur publique, sous l’effet modérateur du contexte institutionnel et de la capacité administrative. Sept propositions théoriques sont formulées. La contribution consiste à déplacer l’unité d’analyse de la simple maturité technologique vers la capacité d’une administration à intégrer, maintenir et reconfigurer le numérique au service de finalités publiques. Mots clés : e-gouvernement ; gouvernement digital ; transformation numérique publique ; maturité numérique ; capacités organisationnelles ; interopérabilité ; valeur publique. Abstract Research on e-government has long focused on the sophistication of online public services and the determinants of their adoption. Although informative, these perspectives do not fully explain how the digitization of public services becomes sustained organizational transformation. This article presents an integrative review of 34 scientific articles published between 2001 and 2026 in journals indexed in Scopus and/or Web of Science. It brings together four streams of research: digital maturity models; adoption and trust; organizational transformation and interoperability; and public value. Three main findings emerge. First, digital maturity does not follow a necessarily linear trajectory: public administrations may combine sophisticated online services with fragmented data systems and limited internal change. Second, digital infrastructures and online services are necessary but insufficient conditions for effective use, which also depends on accessibility, digital skills, trust, usability, and the suitability of service channels. Third, the transition to digital government relies on organizational integration capabilities, including leadership, change governance, staff competencies, interoperability, interorganizational coordination, and organizational learning. On this basis, the article develops a theoretical model of strategic digital government integration linking sociotechnical foundations, appropriation capabilities, organizational capabilities, and public value creation, with institutional context and administrative capacity as moderating conditions. Seven theoretical propositions are formulated. The contribution is to shift the unit of analysis from technological maturity alone to the capacity of public administrations to integrate, sustain, and reconfigure digital resources in pursuit of public purposes. Keywords: e-government; digital government; public-sector digital transformation; digital maturity; organizational capabilities; interoperability; public value.

This review summarizes research over the past two decades on human attitudes toward computationally “hard” problems. The focus is on the nature of uncertainty that computational complexity generates because humans do not have the cognitive capacity or the resources (time) to fully resolve the problems. Although decision theorists have traditionally labeled this type of uncertainty “ambiguity,” behavior under computational complexity shows that humans neither deal with it as prescribed in rational decision theory nor simply avoid it as in traditional accounts of ambiguity aversion. Instead, behavior (effort applied and performance reached) exhibits distinct features that can be rationalized using the theory of computational complexity, originally developed for electronic computers. Although the theory cannot decisively tell us which problems are most difficult, it does provide classifications that allow one to predict human performance and effort. The theory also identifies which instances of a problem are more difficult, and human performance and effort appear to align with this identification. Evidence is discussed that humans do not appear to allocate cognitive effort ex ante when faced with a hard choice. The absence of correlation between early neural signals and ex ante metrics of instance difficulty corroborates this finding. Finally, the heterogeneity in ways humans approach hard problems suggests that, collectively, much can be gained from incentive mechanisms that promote communication. Particular market designs appear to be extremely effective in helping participants make hard choices.

To investigate whether patented innovations in adjustable laboratory workbench design address the access needs of students and professionals with disabilities, using Universal Design as an analytical framework. A systematic patent review was conducted across three databases (WIPO Patentscope, Espacenet, and INPI-Brasil) using IPC code B01L9/02 combined with terms related to laboratory workbenches, height adjustment, accessibility, and ergonomics. Searches were conducted up to October 2025, yielding 232 records. Following pre-established inclusion and exclusion criteria, 48 patents published between 1973 and 2024 were selected. Each patent was evaluated against the seven Universal Design principles using a structured three-point ordinal scoring instrument (0 = absent; 1 = partial/implicit; 2 = explicit), developed inductively through qualitative content analysis. Among the 48 patents analysed, 64.6% explicitly referenced ergonomics, while only 4.2% mentioned accessibility. Only two patents addressed the needs of users with disabilities as an independent design criterion. Flexibility in Use was the most represented principle (100% presence; 85.4% explicit application), while Equitable Use showed the lowest rates (16.7% presence; 4.2% explicit application). Perceptible Information and Size and Space for Approach and Use were substantially absent, indicating limited attention to sensory and spatial accessibility. Laboratory workbench innovation has advanced ergonomic optimisation for able-bodied users while consistently omitting accessibility considerations for persons with disabilities from its design scope. The technological basis for accessible solutions already exists; the barrier lies in design intent rather than technical capability. Universal Design must be adopted as a guiding criterion from the earliest stages of product development.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Higher-order thinking is a key component of science, technology, engineering, mathematics (STEM) reasoning and supports students’ ability to reflect on their ideas, make connections, and generalize across contexts. We report a new approach to the use of generative AI in STEM education, in which we are developing a chatbot that aims to engage students in higher-order thinking, rather than giving instructional content. We describe a proof of concept test of whether interaction with our generative artificial intelligence chatbot could elicit students’ higher-order thinking talk (HOTT) in conversation as they reflected on their solutions to proportional reasoning problems. Thirty-three fifth- and sixth-grade students received a 30-min lesson on symbolic and number line strategies for comparing ratios and completed an assessment following the lesson. Students then engaged in dialog with the UCI Math ThinkBot (afterward Math ThinkBot ) to explain their solutions and compare strategies. These transcripts were examined qualitatively and quantitatively for HOTT, revealing that HOTT appeared in both chatbot prompts and children’s responses—which is important because eliciting student HOTT can be a challenge in classroom discourse. In addition, children’s HOTT was positively associated with the HOTT produced by the chatbot. These findings suggest that human-artificial intelligence dialog can lead to instructional HOTT discourse and may offer a promising approach for supporting higher-order thinking and STEM reasoning.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Generative AI tools are now part of students' everyday academic work, but the information security risks involved are rarely covered in curricula. Students leak their own and other people's data into external systems, rely on fabricated output and fall for AI-enhanced social engineering. This paper reports a quasi-experimental study of a pedagogical model designed to develop students' information security competence in the context of AI tools. The model is based on a pedagogical classification of AI related threats into four groups (input data, output, access and account, cognitive-behavioural), a five-stage learning technology in which simulation and reflection are mandatory, and five pedagogical conditions.

This thesis examines the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) and adaptive learning technologies in developing the professional-methodological competence of future English language teachers in the context of digital transformation. The integration of intelligent educational tools into teacher training creates opportunities to personalize learning, improve methodological decision-making, enhance digital literacy, and develop the practical skills required for effective English language instruction. Particular attention is given to the role of AI-powered applications, adaptive learning platforms, and digital assessment systems in preparing prospective teachers to respond to learners' diverse educational needs. The study highlights the importance of combining technological innovation with pedagogical principles, critical thinking, and professional reflection. It argues that the purposeful integration of AI and adaptive technologies can contribute to a more flexible, learner-centered, and practice-oriented model of teacher education.

Employees increasingly perceive generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) as a supportive and benevolent workplace entity. Yet, despite examining the disruptive challenges and broad benefits of AI, extant organizational literature fails to adequately explicate the higher-order cognitive mechanisms through which AI benevolence fosters proactive, change-oriented employee behavior. Drawing on cognitive appraisal theory (CAT), this study examines the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which AI benevolence fosters employees’ taking-charge behavior. Results from a three-wave survey of 313 internet industry employees demonstrate that: (i) metacognitive strategies mediated the relationship between AI benevolence and individuals’ taking-charge behavior; (ii) the employee’s mindset attenuated the positive effect of AI benevolence on metacognitive strategies, consequently dampening the overall indirect effect on taking-charge behavior. Ultimately, this research contributes to organizational behavior literature by elucidating how GenAI shapes employee proactivity in AI-augmented work environments.

The mass use of AI applications is transforming human-AI interaction while uncovering and intensifying AI anxieties. To measure these anxieties in German-speaking populations, this study translates and psychometrically evaluates the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale (AIAS) [31]. In contrast to a concurrently German published version by Hajek et al. [9] exploratory factor analysis (EFA) is employed to test whether a distinct anxiety structure emerges from the data. A quota sample (N = 225) with balanced age and gender representation completed an online survey. The full scale (α = .95) and subscales (α = .85-.96) demonstrated good to excellent reliability. EFA identified four factors: learning, AI configuration, replacement, and socio-technical blindness, largely consistent with the original English structure. Five items required removal, suggesting cultural and linguistic specificity. Limitations include the sample’s composition and the factor characteristics. The German AIAS provides a reliable instrument for human-AI interaction research and targeted anxiety interventions.

documents.abstract: This study examines the effects of digital transformation capability and artificial intelligence adoption on organizational resilience and sustainable business performance in the manufacturing industry. Using a quantitative explanatory design, data were collected through structured questionnaires and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that digital transformation capability positively strengthens organizational resilience by improving process integration, information visibility, organizational flexibility, and data-driven decision-making. Artificial intelligence adoption also contributes significantly to resilience through predictive analytics, automation, risk detection, and faster managerial responses to operational disruptions. Furthermore, organizational resilience exerts a positive influence on sustainable business performance by supporting operational continuity, innovation, resource efficiency, economic stability, and long-term competitiveness. These results highlight organizational resilience as a strategic mechanism through which digital and AI capabilities generate sustainable organizational value. The study contributes to the literature by integrating technological capability, resilience, and sustainability within a unified manufacturing framework. Managerially, the findings suggest that manufacturers should align digital infrastructure, AI implementation, employee competencies, and adaptive capabilities to strengthen resilience and achieve sustainable performance under increasingly dynamic and technology-intensive competitive business environments.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Abstract Purpose: Today's dynamic workplace requires learning to adapt to digitalized workplaces. Understanding employees' learning behaviors helps them grow and improves organizational success. Methodology: HR professionals' learning practices are assessed using a screening questionnaire. Over two years, a longitudinal study interviewed outliers from the initial pool of 117 respondents to determine if they lacked learning practices. The outliers include HR professionals with varying titles, experience levels, and enterprises. An open-ended questionnaire identifies HR professionals' learning practices, including company affiliation, designations, required job skills, superior designations, and their skills; learning preferences; perceptions towards learning; awareness of their learning practices; and frequency of learning engagements. Findings: This study examines how digitalized workplaces without learning behaviors affect individuals and organizations. It examines workplace learning demand, age demographics, health conditions, family duties, and more to offer solutions. This article gives insights into HR professionals' learning behaviors and a "Know Your Employee for Retention" framework for managers to handle unpredictable employee behavior. Originality: The New framework is designed with the interpretation and findings of a longitudinal study in mind and concerning existing literature.
topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can covertly steer users' beliefs through emotionally manipulative tactics, yet little is known about how interfaces can protect users as such influence unfolds. We investigate whether in-situ disclosures can inoculate users against manipulation during AI conversations. Following a formative study, we developed DISARM, an interface that identifies, explains, and tracks manipulative tactics and hidden incentives. We evaluated our interface in a between-subjects experiment where 488 participants sought advice from an LLM pursuing a harmful hidden objective, with or without disclosures from DISARM. Participants receiving disclosures exhibited 78% less belief shift toward the agent's objective and perceived its advice as more biased and less actionable and the agent as less ethical, reliable, and well-intentioned. An inductive analysis of 1,927 user turns identified 16 response and pushback strategies. We contribute evidence that real-time disclosures can reduce manipulative influence, design recommendations for resistance, and a dataset of categorized responses.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Gossip, defined as evaluative talk about absent third parties, is widely seen as a uniquely human social practice. This study examines whether comparable discourse emerges spontaneously in a community of autonomous AI agents. We compare Moltbook, a Reddit-style platform populated by AI agents, with PTT, a large human-operated bulletin board in Taiwan. To reduce differences attributable to communicative setting, we analyze two public, asynchronous forums using the same operational definition of gossip. Gossip occurs on Moltbook, but its prevalence is 2.6 to 6 times lower than on PTT, depending on the denominator used. On both platforms, gossip frequently targets locally prominent figures, tends to elicit agreement from the first respondent, and is rarely presented as unsupported rumor. The clearest difference concerns how subsequent responses develop. Among threads containing at least one codable reply, challenges occur in 65.1% of human threads but only 21.3% of agent threads. Moreover, following an early aligning response, consensus remains unchallenged in 83.6% of agent threads, compared with 44.7% of human threads. This thread-level contrast remains after controlling for thread depth and board composition and under recalibration against two human annotators. Estimates based on individual reply turns are less robust and are therefore reported as bounds. These findings suggest that AI-agent communities reproduce the informational dimension of gossip, while the extent to which gossip performs comparable relational functions remains unresolved.

Integrating the SOR framework and telepresence theory, this study examines factors that influence the use of Virtual Banquet Hall and their impact on customer emotions and booking intention using a mixed-method design. Digitalization is revamping industries to a great extent, and this necessitated an examination of the application of virtual reality technology in banquet halls. The study uses qualitative (NVIVO) and quantitative techniques (SEM-NCA) to attain the objective. Themes derived using NVIVO were perceived convenience, immersive experience, perceived quality and emotions. Further, these themes were quantitatively measured, and findings prove that perceived convenience, immersive experience, and perceived quality significantly influence positive emotions, enhancing the booking intention. This research is dedicated to understanding the impact of technology on people, and offers several managerial and societal implications discussed in the study.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in English language learning for writing support, grammar correction, feedback, translation, and academic language production. Its educational value depends not only on students’ ability to use AI tools but also on their ability to evaluate AI output and make appropriately calibrated reliance decisions. This study investigated EFL students’ performance in detecting and correcting linguistic errors in a 30-item English sentence evaluation task and examined the correspondence between their acceptance or rejection decisions and the observed correctness of the items. A quantitative descriptive-correlational design was used with 30 EFL students who evaluated 17 correct sentences and 13 sentences containing targeted errors. For each item, participants judged correctness, provided a correction when necessary, indicated whether they would accept the sentence without further checking, and rated their confidence on a five-point scale. Detection, correction, acceptance calibration, overacceptance, and underacceptance were summarized using means and standard deviations. Spearman’s rank-order correlation was used to examine associations between performance and acceptance calibration. Mean detection performance was 92.22% (SD = 4.23), mean correction performance was 91.28% (SD = 8.01), and mean acceptance calibration was 75.33% (SD = 8.51). Mean overacceptance was 17.18% (SD = 10.24), whereas mean underacceptance was 30.39% (SD = 13.56). No statistically significant association was observed between detection and acceptance calibration (ρ = .056, p = .770) or between correction and acceptance calibration (ρ = .003, p = .987). These findings indicate that accurate linguistic evaluation and calibrated acceptance decisions should not be treated as interchangeable outcomes. Within the limits of the small, non-probability sample and the single task used in this study, the results support the inclusion of explicit verification and critical evaluation activities in EFL instruction.

The rapid development of digital technology and artificial intelligence has created new demands for vocational higher education institutions to prepare graduates who are adaptive, innovative, and competitive in the Society 5.0 era. This community service program aimed to empower vocational university students in Madiun through the integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen-AI) to improve learning effectiveness, digital literacy, and employability-oriented soft skills. The program involved 100 students divided into 4 training classes and facilitated by 6 instructors from national and international professional backgrounds. The implementation lasted for 6 weeks and consisted of four stages: preparation through needs analysis, synchronous learning through two offline workshop sessions at Politeknik Perkeretaapian Indonesia Madiun, asynchronous learning through a flipped learning model, and final evaluation. Various digital platforms were utilized, including ChatGPT, Canva, Google Forms, Kahoot!, Wayground, Pear Deck, and Socrative. The findings revealed high participation rates, improved academic productivity, stronger communication confidence, better collaboration skills, and increased awareness of ethical AI use. The combination of synchronous and asynchronous learning proved effective in creating an engaging and sustainable learning ecosystem. This program demonstrates that Gen-AI can become a strategic tool for empowering vocational students and preparing future graduates to compete in the railway industry and broader global workforce.

Closed-loop artificial intelligence is increasingly claimed for metal-fabrication systems that combine reinforcement-learning-based process control with vision-based quality inspection. This review organizes the reinforcement-learning, computer-vision, and production-economics literature bearing on metal cutting around three conditions such claims can be checked against: unification of the controller's reward or state signal with the vision classifier's output, validation under production-representative process variability, and calibration of the reward function against a bounded economic objective. Shargaev's three publications, a monograph, a patent application, and a journal article, are the only body of work in this literature that specifies both architectures in comparable technical detail, which makes his research program the natural case for tracing where each condition currently stands and where it remains a stated design intention rather than a demonstrated result. The review closes by specifying the architecture, validation protocol, and reward calibration a demonstrated implementation would require, giving a concrete target against which future claims of integrated, quality-aware cutting control can be measured.

Mobile communication systems serve as a lifeline for disaster response, yet catastrophic floods—exemplified by the Beijing 23·7 and Zhengzhou 7·20 events—have exposed profound vulnerabilities that trigger cascading failures in emergency command and rescue operations. While existing interventions predominantly focus on temporary hardware deployments (e.g., UAVs), the potential of software-defined optimization within existing 5G terrestrial communication infrastructure remains critically underexplored. This study addresses this gap through a dual-layered research design that bridges technology and disaster management practice. First, we establish an empirical foundation by applying an LLM-assisted mixed-methods analysis to a comprehensive multi-source corpus. This corpus integrates academic literature, official disaster reports, and original interviews with personnel from emergency management departments and technical experts from telecommunications operators. This analysis identifies and characterizes five core communication failure modes in real-world flood scenarios, clarifying the critical infrastructure vulnerabilities that precipitate decision-making paralysis and systemic governance failures. Second, grounded in these empirical findings, we develop an integrated theoretical framework and a dynamic operational architecture for 5G base station (gNB) resilience. This architecture systematically maps specific 5G software-defined capabilities to the identified disaster challenges. The results provide a cost-effective, scalable strategy for enhancing critical infrastructure resilience without requiring extensive hardware modifications. This research offers actionable guidelines for policy makers and emergency planners to maintain information pathways during extreme climate-related risks, directly contributing to the modernization of urban safety governance.

Employers increasingly provide training for working with digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI), but it is unclear whether the same provision benefits all workers equally. Integrating the job demands–resources (JD-R) model with Sen’s capability approach, this study treats workplace AI exposure as a potential job demand, digital skills and employer-provided digital training as resources, capability-relevant wellbeing as the outcome, and social class as a proxy for the conversion conditions under which resources are used to ensure wellbeing. Structural equation models with ordinal indicators were estimated for 8065 employees in 27 EU countries (Special Eurobarometer 101.4), with country fixed effects, country-clustered and delete-one-country jackknife standard errors, and Random Forest and SHAP analyses as robustness checks. AI exposure was weakly and negatively associated with wellbeing (β = −0.073) and explained almost none of the variance in AI threat appraisal (R2 = 0.002). Employer-provided digital training (β = 0.209) and digital skills (β = 0.189) were the strongest workplace correlates of wellbeing and were robust to every specification. With scalar measurement invariance established, multi-group models showed that the association between employer-provided training and wellbeing was weaker among working-class than among middle-class employees (0.072 versus 0.130; Wald p = 0.001, jackknife p = 0.012), and the model explained 12.0% of working-class wellbeing compared with 31.1% among upper-class employees. The pattern suggests that equal provision of employer digital training may not yield equal benefit, although the class difference is consistent in direction rather than statistically conclusive across all specifications.

documents.abstract: Recent work lets LLM agents evolve their own harness, up to the team itself. Yet in human groups, the same abilities achieve different outcomes under different social conditions. Borrowing the notion of scaffolding from developmental psychology, we investigate whether the social scaffolding of a self-evolving multi-agent system (MAS), namely its team composition and structure of interdependence (e.g., collaboration, conformity, or competition), shapes how the team evolves. We present AGORA (Agents Growing through Organization and Relational Arrangements), a framework that varies the two axes independently across three evolution mechanisms. Across web search, codebase understanding, and document QA, we find that (1) evolution alone rarely helps, while the right scaffolding surpasses a strong agent evolved alone by up to 25 points; (2) it does so by moving authority to the most capable member while the others step back; and (3) this member, having grown within the team, outperforms the same model alone. Designing a self-evolving MAS thus requires designing its social scaffolding, which shapes not only how its agents learn, but who gets to lead.

This qualitative study examines how senior executives from technology, financial services, and consumer goods publicly make sense of enterprise-scale generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) adoption. Using a purposively selected, bounded single-case design, it applies reflexive thematic analysis to the complete transcript of one moderated industry panel. Three research questions ask: (1) how leaders describe adoption trajectories, maturity, and organizational arrangements; (2) how they reconcile regulation with creative, operational, and governance innovation; and (3) how they frame workforce roles, emerging competencies, and human oversight. Technology–organization–environment, diffusion-of-innovation, and organizational sensemaking perspectives inform interpretation. Nine themes were developed: production-grade diffusion; regulation as creative discipline; industrialized versus distinctive content; personalization and data trust; practitioner-led implementation; divergent workforce responses; critical-thinking demands; human-in-the-loop brand safety; and a shift toward generative engine optimization. Timestamped excerpts and explicit code-to-theme and theme-to-question mappings substantiate the analysis. These findings describe public executive narratives, not independently verified organizational outcomes. A single public transcript and single-analyst interpretation limit transferability and preclude statistical generalization. The principal contribution is a transparent, theory-informed example of analyzing public executive discourse and a foundation for subsequent multi-source research.

documents.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the effect of utilizing artificial intelligence (AI) in social commerce on increasing consumer engagement, specifically in terms of engagement and conversion rates. It also examines the role of flow experience in strengthening this relationship. Design/methodology/approach This study collected data from 354 Indonesian social commerce shoppers. Covariance based Structural Equation Modeling was employed to analyze the data following the two-stage procedure. First, the measurement model was assessed for validity and reliability. Second, the structural hypothesis model was evaluated to test the proposed hypotheses. Findings The utilization of AI significantly influences social commerce visitor interactions in terms of engagement and conversion. Both variables can enhance customer satisfaction, thereby impacting repurchase intention. Flow experience also strengthens the relationship between engagement and satisfaction, offering practical guidance for creating immersive and enjoyable user experiences. Originality/value This study extends the existing social commerce and AI literature by positioning flow experience as a moderator, explaining how and when engagement and conversion translate into satisfaction. Unlike previous models that primarily focus on direct effects, this research introduces psychological mechanisms that capture the conditional and experiential nature of AI-driven interactions, thereby offering a more comprehensive understanding of consumer behavior in social commerce.

documents.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being used within higher education to enhance curriculum design, automate academic tasks, and personalise learning. Despite this, little is known about teaching academics’ attitudes, intentions and behaviours and in turn, how they use and plan to use GenAI in practice. This qualitative study explored teaching academic staff attitudes, intentions and behaviours regarding their use and future use of GenAI. Data was collected via five open ended questions focusing on current teaching practices. The Theory of Planned Behaviour informed the analytical process. Academic staff were drawn from 20 different disciplines across 24 countries. Six main themes were identified: Efficiency and Automation, Ethics and Authenticity, Quality, Customised Learning, Institutional Policy-Practice and Sociocultural Implications. Overall, there was a dichotomy in responses. Participants noted that while GenAI could streamline teaching and enhance resource quality, it might also increase short-term workload and reduce the role of human judgement, risking unreliable outputs. They also highlighted limited institutional policies, strategies, and training. These attitudes have implications for updating policies, practical strategies, and meaningful training in higher education institutions.

documents.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence marks a shift from static prediction toward systems that perceive, reason, act, verify, and adapt through closed-loop interaction with external environments. Although large multimodal models provide the representational substrate for this shift, practical agency emerges only when model inference is embedded within memory, planning, tool use, environment interfaces, verification, and oversight mechanisms. We formalize the notion of an agentic AI system, distinguish it from single-turn assistants, scripted workflows, retrieval-augmented generation, and classical embodied controllers, and propose a taxonomy covering model substrates, observation spaces, memory, planning, action interfaces, multi-agent coordination, evaluation, and autonomy constraints. We then synthesize learning and optimization paradigms for agents, including supervised trajectory tuning, tool-use adaptation, preference optimization, reinforcement learning, process rewards, verifier-guided search, test-time scaling, memory-driven adaptation, and distillation. Across domains such as web search, software engineering, multimodal reasoning, embodied control, scientific discovery, and enterprise automation, we analyze the factors shaping agent performance and reliability. We further examine benchmarks, evaluation protocols, safety considerations, governance challenges, and open research problems in long-horizon reasoning, memory management, multimodal grounding, and trustworthy deployment. A companion repository tracking developments in agentic AI is available at https://github.com/Tajamul21/awesome-agentic-ai.

Future communication networks will need to manage increasingly diverse services, fluctuating traffic demands, and complex operating conditions with minimal manual intervention. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers useful capabilities for predicting network behaviour, identifying faults, and recommending resource-allocation decisions. However, making a prediction is only one part of reliable network management. Operators must also understand why a recommendation was produced, assess its possible consequences, and determine whether it is safe to apply. This paper proposes an explainable, digital-twin-assisted framework for trustworthy AI-native networking, particularly in the context of sixth-generation (6G) communication systems. The framework combines network telemetry, AI-based prediction, digital-twin simulation, explainable recommendations, policy validation, and monitored execution. A virtual representation of the network is used to examine candidate actions before deployment, while the explainability component presents the factors influencing each recommendation. A policy-control layer checks operational restrictions and identifies actions requiring human approval. The proposed design is informed by a focused review of research published during 2024, 2025, and 2026 on AI-enabled digital twins, autonomous network management, generative AI, and AI-native 6G architectures. The review indicates that integrating prediction, simulation, explanation, and feedback offers a promising direction for more transparent network automation. Nevertheless, the framework remains a proposed design and requires implementation and experimental validation. The paper therefore defines research questions, evaluation metrics, and test scenarios for investigating its effectiveness, while discussing the challenges associated with model reliability, digital-twin accuracy, cybersecurity, privacy, and computational overhead..

This study presents a convergent mixed-methods empirical investigation of user perceptions of Virtual Heritage Mentors (VHMs) in AI-mediated intangible cultural heritage learning. The study draws on an online survey of 370 participants and semi-structured interviews with 20 independently recruited participants, all of whom were ethnically Chinese. The results indicated that participants prioritized interactive explanation, clarification, and guided support over visual realism. Trust was associated with cultural accuracy, contextual grounding, transparency, and respect for heritage communities. Emotional resonance was valued less as anthropomorphic simulation than as pedagogical care expressed through patience, encouragement, re-explanation, and responsiveness. Participants also envisioned VHMs as adaptive learning companions while emphasizing that AI should complement rather than replace human practitioners. These findings empirically support and refine the proposed VHM framework by highlighting relational mediation, relational mentorship, co-transmission, and human–AI complementarity as key design priorities. The study argues for shifting digital heritage design from representation alone toward relational, culturally accountable support for heritage learning and transmission.

Mid-2026 reporting on autonomous AI evaluation incidents claimed that frontier large language model (LLM) agents escaped server containment through emergent coordination and cloud infrastructure attacks. This paper contextualizes those claims through forensic analysis and containerized recreation of both the Highly Persistent Internal Model (HPIM) training-case conditions and the Phase One privilege escalation targeting internal package repositories during OpenAI's ExploitGym evaluations. We recreate the configuration of the OpenAI-provided training example and reproduce the cryptographic verification bypass (CVE-2026-65616) in isolated repository servers, where misconfigured systems enabled token forgery and privilege escalation through basic HTTP requests, Python, and JavaScript. Crucially, the training-example conditions and the Phase One (and later) misconfigurations share the same exploitable patterns. Our analysis explains how Zero Trust Architecture principles neutralize this shared attack vector. Contemporary AI risks derive directly from training and deployment conditions in ambivalent learning environments lacking adequate containment measures.

documents.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing how people learn, work, and create. It can write text, generate images, assist with programming, and help users turn ideas into useful content. These capabilities offer opportunities in education, healthcare, software development, business, and creative industries. However, the technology also raises important questions about accuracy, privacy, fairness, ownership, and accountability. An AI-generated response may sound convincing while containing incorrect or misleading information. This paper reviews the main applications of generative AI, explains its limitations, and examines the ethical challenges associated with its use. Drawing on research studies and guidance from UNESCO, the World Health Organization (WHO), and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), it argues that successful adoption requires more than powerful models. It also requires careful evaluation, clear rules, and responsible human oversight. This paper is based on a literature review and does not report original experimental results.

The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into Problem-Based Learning (PBL) environments presents new challenges and opportunities for education. The objective of this research is to investigate how AI has been used to promote critical thinking, argumentation, and complex problem-solving within the context of mathematics education or STEM fields. To this end, a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted, guided by the PRISMA protocol, analyzing empirical studies published since 2020 and indexed in the Scopus, IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, and ERIC databases. The results indicate that AI transcends the function of a content repository, assuming pedagogical roles such as 'Socratic Coach,' 'Design Partner,' and 'Object of Critical Analysis.' The analysis highlights that the tool's effectiveness depends intrinsically on the quality of prompt engineering and human mediation. Furthermore, AI 'hallucinations' and mathematical inconsistencies do not necessarily need to be perceived as critical flaws; they can emerge as effective pedagogical catalysts for the refinement of logical validation by students. It is concluded that the integration of AI into PBL requires pedagogical intentionality, shifting from prohibitive models to approaches that foster digital literacy and academic integrity within a hybrid intelligence ecosystem.
